title: Alexander Birke & Sofie Kjær Schmidt - Art direction and tech art in Sea Of Rifts, a naval RPG
speaker: Alexander Birke & Sofie Kjær Schmidt
talk_title: Art direction and tech art in Sea Of Rifts, a naval RPG
description: Art direction and production for procedural games is tricky. Artists need to understand the technical limitations and opportunities the medium offers, while programmers must create artist friendly workflows that also support the chosen aesthetic, and still have enough time to code the game itself. Last year Alex gave a talk on the procedural world, story, and character generation in Sea Of Rifts. We now want to open the lid on the treasure trove of experience we have gained on how to efficiently create art content for a generated 3D game in terms of direction, workflow, and technical solutions. In the talk we will first cover the overall art goals of the game. Sofie will then cover the specific techniques and design rules used to design the visuals, how we give feedback to each other, and why artists knowing the basics of the technical implementation, is a big win for the whole team. Alex will round off the talk with showing various artist friendly workflows and clever shader and GPU tricks we use to create a lot of visual variation in the game.

We have a streaming world setup which means the only constant data we have for each game object
that is looking static to the player is actually the height and angle but that is still enough
that we can actually derive a random like value from that and we then use that to apply a random

is appealing to us to view. And also we can use the same noise value to change how much light
there is in each house and that also adds life and character. That rotation and random height
is used to dictate where the LG is being placed on the rock and adds a huge amount of variation

it down and that version of the roof would have those corner pillars which was a clever use of
the generator. Another thing that I am also really pleased I finally got to use in a game that people
have actually tried is what I call the sub-tiling system. It is trim sheets combined with nine slice
sprites. Trim sheets is you can use the fact that textures can tile in the width or height or both.
And nine slice splits is that you take an image and splice it into the nine pieces and you can use
that to create corners that don't stretch well and you can stretch the sides. I came up with a way of
combining the two. When we are texturing these buildings for sunken city, we actually have this
large tile set you see here on the right. And then for each vertex we define the position as normal
and then we define an off set to that file we want to show and also define the tile dimensions in the
vertex data. That actually allows the shader to basically take the current UV, offset it, repeat
it with the frequency of the tile dimension, and that way we can actually show a lot of different
textures from one texture. We are not bound to the limitations that stays with the traditional trim
sheet way you have to basically stretch it to the edge. What was really interesting to me is I made
this technique for a game when I was generating the buildings by code but when it was taken ahold
of he was like I don't need to stick to your rules and started using authoff sets and tiling
dimensions. On the left, he used that to create two different window types with the stain glass
even though there is only one he is picking from. It is like a really interesting way that he found
a way to, yeah, get enhanced use out of it. One thing you might run into if you use this technique

way to get around that is that you have to pad each tile and basically like make that repeat
on to itself. This was quite a hassle to figure out back in the day. Thankfully we haven't had
to deal with it much on Sea Of Rifts because of the camera but it is something to be aware of and
something you can script your way out of with a custom texture importer. All right. Paver.

field being displayed underneath. The way to fix that is by adding noise to it. We can just
